title: Associations Between Long-Term High-Altitude Exposure and Cognitive Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Studies on Event-Related Potentials
abstract: Although long-term high-altitude (HA) exposure is associated with cognitive alterations, evidence regarding the corresponding event-related potential (ERP) components is inconsistent, and a systematic synthesis across processing stages is lacking. This meta-analysis synthesized available ERP evidence to examine neurophysiological alterations associated with cognitive processing following long-term HA exposure. The most consistent finding was a reduction in P300 amplitude among the HA groups (g = −0.476). Reduced P100 amplitude was also observed (g = −0.325), although this finding was less robust, with a possible small-study-effect signal. Rotation-related negativity amplitude was more negative in HA groups (g = −0.748), but this estimate was based on only four independent studies. No reliable between-group differences were observed for other evaluated ERP outcomes. Moderator analyses provided limited evidence of systematic moderation and are constrained by low statistical power. Overall, the available evidence is heterogeneous and primarily based on cross-sectional comparisons. These findings suggest possible stage-dependent associations between long-term HA exposure and ERP alterations, although rigorous longitudinal studies using standardized ERP protocols are needed to substantiate these associations.
